rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The story at a glance "The Wish" by Roald Dahl is a story about nothing but a carpet — and it is one of the most suspenseful things in the syllabus. A small boy, home alone with a scabby dog, is told the red spots on the hallway carpet are hot lava. He invents a game: cross the carpet to the door without touching red.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
The entire story is a child's imagination — the carpet game symbolises risk and fear.
Note the open ending: we never learn if he crosses safely; discuss why Dahl chose this.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: The ambiguous ending (did he step on red?) is deliberate — discuss what the open ending suggests about imagination and fear.  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **The boy** is the story's only character, and he is every child at play: rule-maker, risk-taker, self-encourager. Note the details Dahl chooses — the boy alone, the mother's warning about the dog, the game invented out of boredom — and what they build: a child's inner world is as real to him as the floor, and as dangerous.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **The power of imagination** — a carpet becomes a volcano; the theme is the child mind's ability to make law out of play. **Fear and courage** — the boy's fear is real because his game is real to him; courage is shown as the decision to keep moving, one stone at a time.…  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"What was the game the boy played?" (4 marks)** — the carpet as lava, red as death, purple as safety; state the stakes as the boy holds them. **"What happened when the boy jumped?"** — the honest answer is the story's own: we do not see; the narrative cuts to the empty room.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. What is the boy pretending as he crosses the carpet? (1 mark) — that red patches are red-hot coals and black ones snakes.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The plot, retold with an eye on suspense The setup is three facts: the boy is alone (mother out, father out, only the dog — and the dog is scabby and unwanted, which matters), the carpet is enormous in his eyes, and the game has absolute stakes — touch red and you are burned, as if in a volcano.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Suspense** — the story's engine: stakes are imaginary but narrated as absolute, and the pace slows to single steps. Dahl proves that suspense is a matter of *consequence believed*, not danger real. - **Imagination as the story's world** — the entire action happens inside a child's game; the carpet is a volcano because the boy says so, and the narrative honours his law without irony.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: The entire story is a CHILD'S IMAGINATION on a carpet — say this first; the 'snakes' and 'lava' exist only in the boy's mind.  ·  Trick 2: Suspense technique: short sentences, present-tense immediacy, ticking-clock pressure (mother calling) — name two techniques with examples.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. Why does the story end ambiguously? (2 marks) — to leave the reader inside the child's suspense; the game's danger is imaginary yet felt as real.
